h1: Packing beer bottles in your luggage on the flight home
title: Packing Beer Bottles in Your Luggage | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pack beer bottles and cans in checked luggage for the flight home to India, plus the cabin, airline and customs rules to check first.
teaser: A broken bottle of imperial stout in a suitcase is a holiday memory nobody wants. Pack it properly.
standfirst: Bringing beer home from a trip is one of the pleasures of beer travel. Here is how to pack bottles and cans so they survive the hold, plus the rules to check before you buy a case.
sections:
On most international flights, liquids in hand baggage are limited to containers of 100 ml each in a small clear bag. A 330 ml bottle of beer will not pass security in your cabin bag. Beer bought in duty-free after security, in a sealed bag with the receipt, can usually be carried on, but if you change planes it may be screened again at the transfer airport and taken away.

So the realistic option is checked baggage. Under international aviation dangerous goods rules, drinks up to 24% ABV are not restricted in checked baggage. All beer falls well inside that limit. Your airline can still set its own rules, so check before you fly.
Check customs and weight before you buy

India limits how much alcohol a passenger can bring in without paying duty. The allowance and rules can change. Check the current baggage rules from Indian customs before you buy, especially if you are bringing back a case. If you bring in more than the allowance, declare it at the red channel.

State rules can apply after you land too. Some states limit how much alcohol you can carry or hold at home. Rules vary by state and change, so check the current position for your state.

Weight adds up fast. A full 330 ml glass bottle weighs roughly half a kilo. Six bottles can use a big share of an economy baggage allowance.

1. Put each bottle in its own sealed plastic zip bag. If one breaks, the bag holds the beer.
  2. Wrap each bagged bottle in bubble wrap or a thick layer of clothes. Socks and T-shirts work well.
  3. Place the bottles in the centre of the suitcase, away from the walls, surrounded by soft clothing on every side.
  4. Pack them standing upright where you can, so the yeast stays at the bottom.
  5. Fill gaps so nothing can move. A tight case is a safe case.
  6. Use a hard-shell suitcase if you have one.

Reusable padded bottle sleeves are worth buying if you travel for beer often.

If you want to bring home more than a few bottles, it is tempting to ship them. Be careful. Many international couriers will not carry alcohol for private customers. Importing alcohol into India by post or courier brings its own customs and licensing questions. Rules differ by country and change, so check with the courier and with Indian customs before you try. For most travellers, carrying a few bottles in checked baggage is simpler.

Choose what you bring with care. Six bottles you will savour beat a case you end up giving away. Favour beers you cannot buy in India and styles that keep well. A shop near the end of your trip saves you carrying bottles around the country for days.

Keep the receipts. They help at customs if you are asked about the value of what you are bringing in. They also remind you later where you found each beer.

Cans are lighter than bottles and do not shatter. They can dent, so pack them the same way, wrapped and in the middle of the case. Cans also block light completely, which protects hoppy beer from turning skunky.

If the same beer is available in both, buy cans for the flight. Our guide to how to store beer at home covers what to do with them when you land.

The aircraft hold is pressurised. Sealed bottles and cans do not burst from the change in air pressure on a normal flight. Breakage comes from rough handling, so padding matters far more than anything else.

Corked and caged bottles, such as Belgian ales and gueuze, are sturdy but heavy. Keep the wire cage on. Treat old or valuable bottles with extra padding and pack them in your most protected suitcase.
What to buy and what to drink there

Bring home the beers that travel well and that you cannot get in India: strong, dark or bottle-conditioned beers that will keep. Hoppy IPAs fade quickly. Drink those on your trip and bring the stouts, barley wines and Belgian ales home.

When you land, let bottle-conditioned beers rest upright for a few days before opening. Shaken yeast clouds the beer and can make it foam over. Our guide to building a beer flight has ideas for sharing your haul with friends.

If you bought two bottles of the same beer, open one on the trip and one at home. Compare your notes. Travel and time change beer. Learning what changed is a good test of your palate.

Telling fresh from tired, or travel shock from a real fault, takes a trained nose. That is a skill worth building if you travel for beer.

Your first step: before your next trip, check your airline's checked baggage weight limit and the current Indian customs allowance, then pack six zip bags and some bubble wrap.
faqs: Can I carry beer in my hand luggage?
On most international flights, no. Liquids in the cabin are limited to 100 ml containers, so beer goes in checked baggage.
Is beer allowed in checked baggage?
Yes. International dangerous goods rules do not restrict drinks up to 24% ABV in checked baggage, though airlines and customs set their own limits.
How much beer can I bring into India?
India sets a duty-free allowance for alcohol that can change. Check the current customs baggage rules before you travel and declare anything above the limit.
